claims.text: Rapid, controlled annealing at 600–800°C for a short duration will precipitate a fine, ductile secondary phase at grain boundaries and within the matrix of refractory HEAs.
The proposed annealing treatment will enhance ductility and uniform deformability without compromising high strength.
The proposed annealing treatment will preserve impact-induced energy release.
The initial material is a tungsten-based refractory HEA produced by a multistage thermo-mechanical SCCP process and containing coherent δ and γ″ precipitate structures.
The initial material has a yield strength of approximately 1.4–2.0 GPa and uniform tensile elongation of approximately 7–15%.
Annealing at approximately 650–750°C under a controlled atmosphere will permit sub-micrometer diffusion without excessive coarsening or grain growth.
A sufficiently short annealing duration will selectively precipitate a ductile phase while retaining the existing coherent nanoprecipitates.
The structural mediator will be a finely distributed, ductile, likely coherent δ intermetallic precipitate at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The secondary phase will act as a source for dislocation multiplication.
The secondary phase will inhibit crack initiation and propagation at grain boundaries.
Dislocation accommodation and crack suppression by the precipitates will distribute strain more uniformly and delay necking and fracture.
Coherent matrix–precipitate interfaces will help retain high yield strength.
Coherent matrix–precipitate interfaces will preserve impact-induced energy release.
Annealing will produce at least an approximately 5% relative increase in uniform elongation compared with the untreated baseline.
Annealing will cause no statistically significant reduction in yield strength.
Annealing will cause no statistically significant reduction in impact energy absorption.
Untreated SCCP-processed baseline samples exhibit strengths of approximately 1.4–2.0 GPa and uniform ductility of approximately 7–15%.
The benefit should occur only when annealing avoids precipitate coarsening, grain growth, and grain-boundary embrittlement.
The intervention may fail in alloy compositions predisposed to form brittle secondary phases.
The hypothesis is falsified if annealing fails to improve uniform elongation by approximately 5% or causes a significant reduction in yield strength or impact-induced energy release.

contradictions.description: The starting material is already described as containing coherent δ and γ″ precipitates, while the intervention is presented as triggering formation of a newly precipitated phase likely to be δ; the hypothesis does not distinguish new δ precipitation from modification of the pre-existing δ phase.

The energetic endpoint alternates between impact-induced energy release and impact energy absorption. These are not interchangeable measurements, so the proposed measurement of absorption does not directly test the stated preservation of energy release.
